a1196 body: Tantalus "tried to steal it for mortals" → "stole it for his mortal friends", per Pindar's First Olympian Ode (476 BC); the pool-and-fruit punishment is now called the best-known version; added the origin of "to tantalize" / Tantalusqualen — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tantalus ; Hebe introduced as goddess of youth, with the Iliad's nectar-pouring — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebe_(mythology)
a1196 notes: reworded to point to the printed card (the wording no longer calls ambrosia a plant)
Russian added.
Images added.
Proofread (reasons in the entries above / the batch report).

diff: daughter of Zeus and Hera, and
In the "Iliad" it is Hebe who pours the gods their nectar.
mortal friends – the crime Pindar gives him in his First Olympian Ode of 476 BC –
In the best-known version of his punishment he stands in a pool beneath fruit trees, with water and fruit forever receding from his grasp, which is why English still says "to tantalize".
Tochter von Zeus und Hera, und
In der „Ilias“ ist es Hebe, die den Göttern den Nektar einschenkt.
– das Vergehen, das ihm Pindar in seiner Ersten Olympischen Ode von 476 v. Chr. zuschreibt –,
In der bekanntesten Fassung seiner Strafe steht er in einem Teich unter Obstbäumen, und Wasser und Früchte weichen immer vor seinem Griff zurück – daher sprechen wir bis heute von Tantalusqualen.
